propositions.text: The appellants are Mexican citizens appealing the RPD's August 20, 2019 decision rejecting their refugee claims under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Mexico, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 20, 2019, rejecting their refugee protection claims made under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The appellants, Mexican citizens, appeal the RPD's August 20, 2019 decision rejecting their refugee claims under IRPA sections 96 and 97, court states.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was appointed designated representative of the minor children, whose claims are based on his.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was appointed as the designated representative of the minor children, whose claims are based on his.

paragraphs.summary: The male appellant was appointed designated representative of the minor children, whose claims depend on his, court states.

propositions.text: The male appellant alleges assaults and death threats by Jalisco cartel members for reporting a crime to police.
propositions.quote: The male appellant alleges that he was the victim of assaults and death threats by members of the Jalisco cartel, because he reported them to the police for a crime he had witnessed.

paragraphs.summary: The male appellant alleges assaults and death threats by Jalisco cartel members for reporting a crime, appellant says.

propositions.text: On Feb 11, 2016, male appellant saw cartel members remove a bloodied person, called police who arrested one member.
propositions.quote: He alleges that, on February 11, 2016, he saw three cartel members named XXXX, XXXX and XXXX remove a person who was covered in blood from their vehicle and put the individual in the trunk. The male appellant called police, who arrested XXXX, one of the members.

propositions.text: Same day, male appellant was attacked and threatened by a cartel member for reporting to police; he filed a police complaint.
propositions.quote: The same day, he was attacked by XXXX, who threatened to kill him, as well as his family, for reporting them to police. The male appellant made a police complaint so that the events would be investigated.

paragraphs.summary: The male appellant saw cartel members abduct a bloodied person, called police who arrested one; he was attacked and threatened, then filed complaint, appellant says.

propositions.text: Next day, cartel members threatened male appellant's wife to withdraw complaint and broke their home's windows.
propositions.quote: The next day, XXXX and XXXX went to the male appellant's home and threatened his wife to make them withdraw the complaint or they would regret it. They then broke the windows of their home.

propositions.text: On Feb 15, 2016, appellants sought refuge at male appellant's sister-in-law's house.
propositions.quote: On February 15, 2016, the appellants left to seek refuge in a house that belonged to the male appellant's sister-in-law.

paragraphs.summary: Cartel members threatened the wife to withdraw complaint and broke windows; appellants sought refuge at sister-in-law's house, appellant says.

propositions.text: On May 9, 2018, female appellant was accosted by a cartel member who tried to take her baby; she escaped with help.
propositions.quote: On May 9, 2018, while the female appellant was on her way to the pediatrician with the baby, she was accosted by XXXX, who attempted to take the baby from her. She escaped with the help of people on the street who came to her aid.

paragraphs.summary: Female appellant was accosted by cartel member trying to take her baby; she escaped with help, appellant says.

propositions.text: On May 11, 2018, male appellant's sister-in-law found their home's windows broken and a threatening note.
propositions.quote: On May 11, 2018, the male appellant's sister-in-law found the windows of the home where she was housing the appellants broken and a note indicating [translation] "I know where you live."

paragraphs.summary: Sister-in-law found their home's windows broken and a threatening note on May 11, 2018, appellant says.

propositions.text: On May 12, 2018, appellants sought refuge at male appellant's grandmother's home, then left Mexico for Canada claiming refugee protection.
propositions.quote: On May 12, 2018, the appellants sought refuge at the home of the male appellant's grandmother. They then left Mexico on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, for Canada, where they claimed refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants sought refuge at grandmother's home, then left Mexico for Canada claiming refugee protection, appellant says.

propositions.text: Appellants still fear for their lives if returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: The appellants still fear for their lives should they return to Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants fear for their lives if returned to Mexico, appellant says.

propositions.text: RPD rejected claims, finding appellants had internal flight alternative in Mérida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claims, concluding that they had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in the towns of Mérida or Campeche.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred in assessing risk in IFA cities and ask RAD to allow appeal or order new hearing.
propositions.quote: The appellants submit that the RPD erred in assessing their prospective risk in the IFA cities. The appellants are asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow the appeal or to order a de novo hearing before another member.

paragraphs.summary: RPD rejected claims due to internal flight alternative; appellants argue RPD erred and ask RAD to allow appeal or order new hearing, parties say.

propositions.text: After independent analysis, RPD erred in IFA assessment; set aside RPD decision and find appellants need protection under IRPA section 97.
propositions.quote: After conducting an independent analysis of all the evidence on the record, including the recording of the hearing, I conclude that the RPD erred in its IFA assessment. Consequently, I set aside the RPD's determination, substitute a determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, and find that the appellants are persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD erred in IFA assessment, sets aside decision, and finds appellants need protection under IRPA section 97, court states.

propositions.text: RAD must review RPD decision and conduct own analysis to determine if RPD erred; standard of review is correctness.
propositions.quote: The RAD is required to review the RPD's decision and to conduct its own analysis of all the evidence on the record to determine, in light of the arguments put forward by the appellant, whether the RPD erred. The applicable standard of review in this case is correctness.

paragraphs.summary: RAD must review RPD decision and conduct own analysis to determine if RPD erred; standard of review is correctness, court states.

propositions.text: Credibility is not at issue; RPD found appellants credible and did not err on this point.
propositions.quote: Credibility is not at issue, given that the RPD found the appellants to be credible. I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: Credibility is not at issue; RPD found appellants credible and did not err, court states.

propositions.text: RPD found appellants did not show cartel motivation or ability to pursue them in Mérida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the appellants did not establish that the cartel was motivated to pursue them in the proposed IFA cities, namely, Mérida or Campeche, or that it had the ability to do so.

propositions.text: Court finds RPD erred in its analysis of the evidence regarding cartel's motivation and ability in IFA cities.
propositions.quote: I am of the view opinion that the RPD erred in its analysis of the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found no cartel motivation or ability to pursue appellants in IFA cities; court finds RPD erred in this analysis.

propositions.text: RPD found cartel waited two years before attempting to find appellants, so no motivation to pursue them.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the fact that the cartel members [translation] "waited two years before showing up, attempting to grab the baby from the female claimant's hands on May 9, 2018," does not establish that they would be motivated to locate them should they return to Mexico.

propositions.text: RPD stated criminals did not show interest in finding male claimant to kill or harm him, balancing probabilities.
propositions.quote: the panel concludes, on a balance of probabilities, that the criminals in question did not demonstrate an interest in finding the male claimant to kill him or otherwise go after him.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found cartel waited two years before attempting to find appellants and thus lacked motivation to pursue them, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: Evidence shows appellants lived in León, not Acapulco; they sought refuge nearby but assailants found them two years later.
propositions.quote: First, the evidence reveals that the male appellant and his family lived in the city of Léon, in the state of Guanajuato, where the incidents occurred, not in Acapulco. According to their written account and their testimony, the appellants left their home on February 15, 2016, to seek refuge in a house that belonged to the female appellant's sister, an hour away from their home. According to them, they could not afford to move to another part of the country. Although the house was in the same city, there is no evidence on the record that their assailants knew this new location, as the RPD indicates. The evidence reveals only that the cartel members found them at this location two years later.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds appellants lived in León, not Acapulco; sought refuge nearby; assailants found them two years later, court states.

propositions.text: Cartel's pursuit two years later shows motivation to intimidate appellants to withdraw complaint, shown by attempted baby abduction and threats.
propositions.quote: In addition, the fact that the cartel members pursued them two years after the events shows that they were motivated to do so and, at the very least, to intimidate them into withdrawing their police complaint. This is clear from the attempted abduction of the baby on May 9, 2018, when the female appellant was on her way to the pediatrician, and from the fact that their assailants went to their new residence, broke the windows and left a note indicating [translation] "I know where you live."

paragraphs.summary: Court finds cartel's pursuit two years later shows motivation to intimidate appellants, evidenced by baby abduction attempt and threats.

propositions.text: Passage of two years is not determinative; cartel motivation to intimidate or eliminate witness remains likely given low prosecution rates.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that the passage of two years is not a determinative factor in assessing their assailants' interest in going after the appellants, should they return to Mexico. This does not, in my opinion, make it less likely that they would be motivated to intimidate or eliminate a potential witness. This is especially true in light of the documentary evidence indicating that Mexico has "extremely low rates of prosecution for all forms of crime," and prosecutions "could take years to complete."

paragraphs.summary: Court finds two-year delay is not determinative; cartel motivation remains likely given low prosecution rates in Mexico.

propositions.text: Jalisco cartel is powerful and violent; Mexican government declared it one of most dangerous with extensive reach in 2015.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, it is worth noting that the Jalisco cartel is extremely powerful and violent. The objective evidence indicates that, in "2015, the Mexican government declared CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in the country and one of two with the most extensive reach."

propositions.text: Complaints to state authorities against gangs lead to pressure to drop complaint and almost certainly death if not complied with.
propositions.quote: It also indicates "that making a complaint to a state authority against a gang would lead to pressure to drop the complaint and 'almost certainly' lead to death if the individual did not comply."

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Jalisco cartel is powerful and violent; complaints to authorities lead to pressure and likely death if not dropped.

propositions.text: Based on evidence and incidents, court finds it more likely than not that persecutors remain interested in pursuing appellants who filed complaint.
propositions.quote: On the basis of this evidence and the incidents experienced by the male appellant, I conclude that it has been established that it is more likely than not that the agents of persecution are still interested in pursuing the appellants who filed a complaint against them.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes it is more likely than not that persecutors remain interested in pursuing appellants who filed complaint, court states.

propositions.text: The RPD did not consider all documentary evidence about Jalisco cartel's ability to find appellants in Mérida or Campeche.
propositions.quote: As the appellants submit, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not take into account all of the documentary evidence with respect to the Jalisco cartel's ability to find the appellants should they return to Mérida or Campeche.

propositions.text: The RPD's conclusion on the cartel's ability to find appellants is erroneous.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RPD's conclusion in this regard is erroneous.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the RPD ignored evidence on Jalisco cartel's reach; the court finds the RPD's conclusion erroneous.

propositions.text: The RPD found Jalisco cartel operates in 14 states, not in Mérida or Yucatan, so claimant did not prove cartel's ability to find him in Mexico.
propositions.quote: In the panel's view, although the Jalisco cartel wields undeniable influence, the documentary evidence on Mexico reveals that its activities are limited to the central part of the country and that it operates in only 14 states in all. The cartel is not active in Mérida or in Yucatan, for example, states with some of the lowest crime rates in Mexico, according to the documentary evidence. On this basis, the panel concludes that the male claimant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the Jalisco cartel's ability to find him anywhere in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Jalisco cartel limited to 14 states, not active in Mérida or Yucatan, so claimant failed to prove risk.

propositions.text: Tab 7.2 shows Jalisco cartel expanded to 22 states and has national reach despite leadership losses.
propositions.quote: Tab 7.2 contains the following information regarding the presence and influence of Jalisco in Mexico: ... it has a presence in 22 of 32 Mexican states.... Recently, some analysts have identified Cartel Jalisco-New Generation as a cartel with national reach.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes evidence that Jalisco cartel has expanded to 22 states and has national reach.

propositions.text: Even if IFA cities are outside Jalisco's area, evidence shows cartel can find victims anywhere in Mexico.
propositions.quote: Even if the proposed IFA cities are outside Jalisco's area of operation, I agree with the appellants that the objective evidence establishes that the Jalisco cartel has the ability to find its victims anywhere in the country.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the cartel can find victims anywhere in Mexico, even outside its usual area.

propositions.text: Evidence states gangs can track people outside their area using corrupt law enforcement and rely on representation in other areas.
propositions.quote: The evidence states that "a large debt or a personal vendetta could motivate a gang to track someone outside their area, and that gangs can use 'corrupt law enforcement agents' to obtain information about people they pursue." The evidence also establishes that "in order to extend their influence beyond their areas of operation, cartels rely on the 'representation' they have in other areas."

paragraphs.summary: Evidence shows gangs track people outside their area using corrupt police and rely on representation elsewhere.

propositions.text: Jalisco cartel has strategic alliances with Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel, which influence Yucatán Peninsula where IFA cities are.
propositions.quote: It specifically notes that Jalisco has "developed 'strategic alliances' with groups in other regions, including Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel splinter groups along the Gulf Coast." According to the "Stratfor Cartel Map by region of Influence (2018)," ... the Tamaulipas, Los Zetas remnants and Gulf Cartel remnants groups are present and have influence in the Yucatán Peninsula, where the two proposed IFA cities are located.

propositions.text: The map shows all of Mexico is under cartel influence.
propositions.quote: Moreover, this map shows that all of Mexico is under the influence of cartels.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Jalisco's alliances extend cartel influence to Yucatán and all Mexico is cartel-influenced.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows Jalisco cartel can locate appellants in Mérida or Campeche via alliances; RPD erred.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, it is my opinion that the documentary evidence establishes that the Jalisco cartel has the ability and resources to locate the appellants in Mérida or Campeche, owing to its alliances with Los Zetas and Cartel del Golfo. Therefore, the RPD erred on this point.

propositions.text: Jalisco cartel can locate appellants elsewhere in Mexico through alliances; threats target entire family.
propositions.quote: Jalisco also has the ability to locate the appellants in another part of Mexico through its alliances with other cartels that are present throughout the country. In my opinion, even though the principal appellant was the only one who witnessed the crime committed by the Jalisco members, the death threats and acts of intimidation were directed against the entire family.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Jalisco cartel can locate appellants anywhere in Mexico and threats target the whole family; RPD erred.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, all appellants face risk to life or unusual treatment if returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: Consequently, I conclude that it has been established, on a balance of probabilities, that all the appellants would be subjected to a risk to their lives or to unusual treatment or punishment should they return to Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes appellants face risk to life or unusual treatment if returned to Mexico.

propositions.text: State lacks power to protect victims from cartels, which dominate local politicians and governments.
propositions.quote: The objective evidence shows that the state does not have the power to protect victims pursued by the cartels, which are often more powerful than the public authorities. Sources note that organized crime organizations "seek to dominate and intimidate local politicians" and "control local administration budgets" or "infiltrate[e] local governments and law enforcement."

propositions.text: Local police officers have been shot after attending threatened families.
propositions.quote: Local newspapers report cases of police officers being shot after attending to families who were threatened by criminals.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the state cannot protect victims as cartels dominate local politicians and police have been attacked.

propositions.text: Evidence shows corruption and collusion of police with criminals; prosecutions are low and slow; witness protection is flawed.
propositions.quote: There is also evidence of the corruption of state officials and the fact that police forces at times collude with criminal groups. As previously mentioned, the prosecution rate for all forms of crime is extremely low and prosecutions can take years to complete. The witness protection program lacks financial resources and has a number of flawed protection measures.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes police corruption, low prosecution rates, and flawed witness protection program.

propositions.text: Evidence rebuts presumption of adequate state protection for cartel victims.
propositions.quote: I am of the opinion that this evidence rebuts the presumption that adequate state protection is available to victims pursued by cartel members.

propositions.text: Male appellant witnessed cartel crime and threats reported to police; police did nothing to protect family.
propositions.quote: In this case, the male appellant witnessed a crime committed by members of the Jalisco cartel and threats against him and his family that he reported to police. The evidence establishes that the cartel members repeatedly threatened the male appellant's family so that he would withdraw his complaint. Despite that, police did nothing to protect the male appellant and his family.

propositions.text: Adequate protection from Jalisco cartel would not be available if appellants return to Mexico.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I conclude that adequate protection from the Jalisco cartel would not be available to the appellants should they return to Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds state protection inadequate as police failed to protect appellant's family despite threats.

propositions.text: Under IRPA, the RPD's decision is set aside and appellants are found persons in need of protection under section 97.
propositions.quote: Under paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, I set aside the RPD's determination and substitute a determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, and I find that the appellants ... are persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court sets aside the RPD decision and finds appellants need protection under IRPA section 97.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal.
